(1998). https://doi.org/10.1016/s0921-8890(98)00029-3 Context: "Faratin, Sierra, and Jennings model time-dependent tactics by making the next offer a function of elapsed time and the negotiation deadline (tmax). An agent's initial offer is determined by a constant xj within the issue's value interval, while the offer function moves toward the issue's reservation value as the deadline approaches. The concession function αj(t) is constrained to remain between 0 and 1, begin at xj, and reach 1 at tmax. Two parameterized families are presented: polynomial and exponential functions, with β controlling the curve's convexity and therefore the timing of concession. Boulware tactics use β < 1 and maintain the initial offer until time is nearly exhausted, then concede toward the reservation value. Conceder tactics use β > 1 and move rapidly toward the reservation value. The excerpt also distinguishes behavior-dependent tactics, which calculate the next offer from the opponent's previous attitude or behavior; it notes that these tactics include different forms of imitation, although their detailed equations are outside the supplied passage. The broader model additionally treats time as a resource and extends the framework to dynamic deadlines and resource-estimation tactics."

Faratin, Sierra, and Jennings classify negotiation tactics according to the criterion used to generate issue values. Time-dependent tactics model concession as a function of the remaining time before a deadline: an agent is expected to concede more rapidly as the deadline approaches. The particular concession curve distinguishes tactics in this family, with the excerpt illustrating polynomial and exponential time functions using relative time t/tmax. Behavior-dependent, or imitative, tactics instead base a counteroffer on the opponent's previous behavior; they vary in what opponent behavior is imitated and how strongly. Such tactics are especially applicable when the agent is not under substantial time pressure and wants to avoid exploitation. The model allows multiple tactics to be combined for one issue through weighted averaging. For example, an agent can combine a time-dependent suggestion with an imitative suggestion, assigning larger weight to the tactic considered more important. The excerpt does not explicitly name the Boulware and Conceder strategies, nor does it provide their exact reservation-value/deadline parameterized equations, but it establishes the framework in which such strategies are represented by different time-dependent concession curves. Offers are evaluated against the agent's scoring function and current prospective counteroffer; an offer is accepted if it scores better, rejected at the deadline, or otherwise answered with a counteroffer.

The excerpt describes two broad classes of evaluation: accuracy measures for the opponent model itself and performance measures for the negotiation strategy using that model. Reported accuracy metrics are primarily point-estimate or association measures. For issue-weight, reservation-value, or other scalar estimates, the survey gives Euclidean distance; it also reports rank disagreement and Pearson correlation for issue-weight vectors. For predicted bidding behavior, it reports mean squared error (MSE/RMSE-related), mean absolute error, percentage error, and correlation. For complete preference profiles, it reports mean absolute utility distance across outcomes, pairwise ranking distance, and Pearson correlation; these metrics can also evaluate acceptance-strategy models by comparing actual and predicted acceptance probabilities for bids. The excerpt notes scalability limitations for all-pairs ranking metrics and suggests Monte Carlo or correlation-based alternatives. It then states that strategy-level evaluation focuses on performance gains from employing the model, with negotiation duration mentioned as another possible measure. This passage contains no mention of proper scoring rules such as log score, Brier score, or CRPS, no calibration diagnostics, and no explicit benchmark protocol beyond the surveyed studies and metric overview tables. raw_entry: [7.1] Distilling Bayesian Belief States into Language Models for Auditable Negotiation. Zongqi Cui, Baihan Lin. ArXiv (2605). https://doi.org/10.48550/arxiv.2605.04507 Context: "The excerpt presents BOND (Bayesian Opponent-belief Negotiation Distillation), a framework for making negotiation agents' beliefs about opponent types explicit and auditable. In the CaSiNo setting, the hidden opponent type is one of six private priority orderings over Food, Water, and Firewood. An LLM-based Bayesian teacher evaluates each dialogue context against these six hypotheses, converts the scores into a posterior distribution, and uses that posterior for accept, reject, or counteroffer decisions. The teacher achieves a mean turn-level Brier score of 0.085 on 150 held-out dialogues and 1,054 predictions. An 8B student is trained to produce negotiation actions alongside normalized posterior beliefs in tagged text; it reaches Brier 0.114, improving substantially over the uniform six-ordering reference of approximately 0.139. A larger 70B structured-chain-of-thought baseline has better accept/reject F1 but much poorer posterior calibration, with Brier 0.194. The paper uses posterior trajectories, belief-versus-policy error decomposition, and posterior-prefix interventions to assess auditability. Its findings suggest that distillation preserves a scoreable and reasonably calibrated belief report, while the causal connection between corrected beliefs and selected actions remains comparatively weak."
title: Distilling Bayesian Belief States into Language Models for Auditable Negotiation
context_quotes: The excerpt presents BOND (Bayesian Opponent-belief Negotiation Distillation), a framework for making negotiation agents' beliefs about opponent types explicit and auditable. In the CaSiNo setting, the hidden opponent type is one of six private priority orderings over Food, Water, and Firewood. An LLM-based Bayesian teacher evaluates each dialogue context against these six hypotheses, converts the scores into a posterior distribution, and uses that posterior for accept, reject, or counteroffer decisions. The teacher achieves a mean turn-level Brier score of 0.085 on 150 held-out dialogues and 1,054 predictions. An 8B student is trained to produce negotiation actions alongside normalized posterior beliefs in tagged text; it reaches Brier 0.114, improving substantially over the uniform six-ordering reference of approximately 0.139. A larger 70B structured-chain-of-thought baseline has better accept/reject F1 but much poorer posterior calibration, with Brier 0.194. The paper uses posterior trajectories, belief-versus-policy error decomposition, and posterior-prefix interventions to assess auditability. Its findings suggest that distillation preserves a scoreable and reasonably calibrated belief report, while the causal connection between corrected beliefs and selected actions remains comparatively weak.

The BOND framework (Bayesian belief-state distillation) separates negotiation into language interpretation, Bayesian belief revision, menu/action selection, and response generation. In the CaSiNo domain, the opponent's hidden type is represented as one of six possible orderings over FOOD, WATER, and FIREWOOD priorities. At each dialogue turn, a LoRA-adapted Llama-3.1-8B model scores how compatible the full dialogue history is with each ordering. These compatibility scores are clipped and temperature-transformed, then combined with the previous posterior under a Bayesian update, using a uniform prior unless otherwise specified. The resulting categorical posterior is used both for opponent-type prediction and for scoring candidate allocations through posterior expected opponent utility. The posterior is evaluated directly with turnlevel Brier score, making calibration and belief quality measurable rather than relying only on negotiation outcomes. In the main teacher evaluation on 1,054 turn-level predictions from 150 held-out dialogues, the reported mean Brier score is 0.085; lower values indicate more accurate probabilistic predictions. The teacher's posterior, intent, selected content, and utterance are distilled into an 8B student that emits tagged structured text, allowing the model's belief state and action rationale to be inspected and audited at every turn. The excerpt does not provide additional calibration metrics such as reliability diagrams or expected calibration error.

BOND distills Bayesian belief states about an opponent's priority ordering into an 8B language model that emits posterior beliefs as tagged text alongside negotiation actions. The excerpt reports that the distilled student preserves much of the Bayesian teacher's posterior calibration, although standard supervised fine-tuning preserves belief reports more reliably than the causal connection from posterior beliefs to actions. In Protocol 3 on 150 held-out CaSiNo dialogues, the table reports Brier-related results for the Bayesian teacher and distilled student, with values shown as 0.048 and 0.190 for the teacher and 0.190 and 0.114 for the student across the displayed evaluation columns; the excerpt's formatting does not identify all column headers. Teacher and student Brier scores are computed from native single-pass posterior outputs, while the 70B baseline's Brier score is derived from majority-vote shares over five self-consistency samples. In a cross-domain Deal-or-No-Deal test, zero-shot renamed transfer achieves a DND-normalized Brier score of 0.1335, compared with 0.3190 for direct posterior prompting; few-shot adaptation improves this to 0.1166. These DND scores use a different normalization from CaSiNo and should only be compared within their respective sections. The posterior is an auditable computational belief state rather than a direct measurement of human mental states.

The excerpt provides a useful ARA distinction for analyzing an opponent in bargaining or negotiation. Aleatory uncertainty concerns randomness in the outcome conditional on the parties' decisions; in the auction illustration, it includes uncertainty about the book's condition and the value realized after bids are made. Epistemic uncertainty concerns what the analyst does not know about the opponent, including the opponent's utility function or valuation, beliefs about outcome probabilities, and available resources. A Bayesian ARA model represents these unknowns with subjective probability distributions, potentially obtained through elicitation. In the auction example, Daphne assigns distributions to Apollo's valuation and to the fraction of that valuation he may bid, then integrates over these uncertainties to obtain a subjective probability of winning and optimize expected utility. This framework can analogously represent uncertainty about an opponent's reservation value in negotiation and support decisions about whether information collection is worthwhile. However, the excerpt does not explicitly define or calculate the value of information, nor does it discuss bargaining-specific reservation values. It does emphasize that analysts must distinguish uncertainty about the opponent's attributes from concept uncertainty— uncertainty about how the opponent makes decisions—and can model nonstandard or boundedly rational behavior.

It distinguishes two forms of uncertainty in opponent modeling: aleatoric uncertainty, caused by intrinsic randomness in an opponent's actions, and epistemic uncertainty, caused by the difficulty of inferring complex behavioral patterns. UAOM addresses these uncertainties with a hybrid behavior-modeling module that combines probabilistic and deterministic networks in an ensemble. The probabilistic network represents the opponent's behavior as a distribution and captures aleatoric randomness, rather than producing only a single deterministic action prediction. The ensemble of models improves epistemic capacity by representing uncertainty associated with limited or incomplete knowledge of complicated opponent behaviors. UAOM also addresses uncertainty introduced when the opponent model is used by the downstream reinforcement-learning policy. Its opponent-aware dynamic modeling approach learns environmental dynamics in the presence of opponents, reducing the impact of uncertain opponent-model predictions on the controlled agent's Markov dynamics and learning process. The reported experiments cover simulated opponents with varying randomness in cooperative, competitive, and mixed-motive games, as well as human-agent interaction tasks. Results reportedly show particularly strong improvements over baselines when opponent randomness is high.

The excerpt presents Uncertainty-Aware Opponent Modeling (UAOM), a framework for deep reinforcement learning that explicitly addresses two forms of uncertainty in opponent modeling. Aleatoric uncertainty arises from intrinsic randomness or high stochasticity in an opponent's behavior, while epistemic uncertainty concerns limitations in representing complex and diverse behavioral strategies. UAOM uses a Hybrid Behaviour Modeling Module combining deterministic and probabilistic networks. Both networks share a recurrent encoder that processes the controlled and modeled agents' history trajectories into an opponent behavioral embedding. The deterministic decoder predicts the opponent's exact observation and action trajectories, supporting the representation of structured and complex behavior. The probabilistic decoder models observations with a Gaussian distribution and actions with a Gumbel distribution, using reparameterized sampling to preserve trainability. This probabilistic component captures behavioral randomness and predicts distributions rather than single deterministic actions; observation outputs are trained with mean squared error, while action distributions use negative log-likelihood. The ensemble is intended to improve cognitive representation and mitigate epistemic uncertainty without losing the ability to model aleatoric variability. UAOM also adds opponent-aware dynamic modeling so that transition dynamics affected by opponent actions can provide more consistent features for downstream reinforcement learning.
